title: Has AI Proved the Riemann Hypothesis? What It Means and What's Next
summary: A mathematician working with Claude proved the Riemann hypothesis, a problem many thought was beyond AI. What it means and what's next.
body_markdown:
Earlier this year, mathematicians using AI tools announced they had solved a Millennium Prize Problem related to the Navier-Stokes equation.


In October, OpenAI released a result on prime numbers that Scientific American called the first crack in the Riemann hypothesis.


Then on November 20, 2026, Levent Alpöge, a mathematician at Anthropic, announced that he had proved the Riemann hypothesis itself, working with Claude.


The Riemann hypothesis is one of the hardest unsolved problems in mathematics, and many mathematicians believed it was beyond the reach of AI. A day after the announcement, the Lean and Mathlib communities[certified that the proof is correct](https://leanprover-community.github.io/blog/posts/riemann-hypothesis/) .


Mathematicians have yet to fully understand the argument, but the result is the strongest sign yet that AI can create new knowledge at the frontier of a field.


## What is the Riemann hypothesis?


The Riemann hypothesis is a prediction about prime numbers, the numbers like 2, 3, 5, 7 and 11 that can only be divided by 1 and themselves. Bernhard Riemann made it in 1859.


Primes look scattered at random. After 23, the next prime is 29, and after 29 it's 31. Riemann predicted that underneath, they follow a precise pattern in how they're spread out.


Mathematicians have tested the prediction on enormous numbers of cases, and it has held every time. The hard part is proving it holds for every number, all the way to infinity.


It is one of the seven Millennium Prize Problems chosen by the Clay Mathematics Institute, which offers $1 million for a solution. Many mathematicians consider it the most important open problem in the field.


## Why is the Riemann hypothesis so important?


It is one of the hardest problems in mathematics. Generations of mathematicians tried to prove it after Riemann proposed it, and many expected a proof would need whole new areas of theory to be built first.


That made it a test for AI. A common argument held that language models only[stitch together patterns from their training data](https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/3442188.3445922) without understanding them, so they couldn't produce new ideas. As recently as February, Scientific American described the problems AI had helped solve as minor ones.


Few mathematicians expected that to change with Riemann. In an earlier interview, MIT mathematician Andrew Sutherland told Scientific American that an AI able to prove it "is not one I'd want to meet." Abhishek Saha of Queen Mary University of London wrote that, like most mathematicians, he had believed it was out of reach even with the best AI tools.


Alpöge says the proof draws on far more mathematics than he ever imagined it would need. To Saha, it looks like an unexpected shortcut through areas of math that were built for other problems. Either way, it's new mathematics. And it was found with an AI, on a problem experts thought AI couldn't touch.


## Has AI proved the Riemann hypothesis?


Levent Alpöge says he has, together with Claude. In a[four-page note](https://alpo.ge/remark.pdf) , he explains that he steered the work toward the right setting, based on a simpler test case, and then Claude "began to leave me in awe." He also says the method extends to a broader version of the problem, the Generalized Riemann Hypothesis.


The full argument ran past 250,000 pages. Alpöge judged a document that size unreadable, so he released it as 17 million lines of code in Lean instead. Lean is a programming language for mathematical proofs, and it only accepts a proof when every step follows from the ones before it.


Over the next day, dozens of people ran the code and got the same result. Sutherland compiled it himself and told Scientific American he sees almost no chance that anything is wrong. On November 21, the Lean and Mathlib communities said they are fully confident the proof is correct.


A second proof appeared the same day. Stanford mathematician Ravi Vakil posted a[human-written preprint by Alessandro Maria Masullo](https://www.nature.com/articles/d41586-026-03812-7) , who avoided getting feedback from chatbots while writing it. Masullo says he is still fixing some problems in it, and checks on his proof are ongoing.


## What happens if the Riemann hypothesis is solved?


For mathematics, it's a landmark. Oxford number theorist James Maynard told Nature that once mathematicians understand the argument, it "will surely be viewed as one of the absolute pinnacles of mathematical results."


Hector Pasten of the Pontifical Catholic University of Chile compared it to a Rosetta Stone in an interview with Scientific American, because it connects different branches of math.


That understanding will take a while. Terence Tao wrote on his blog that digesting it will take some time. Andrew Granville of the University of Montreal told Nature that Alpöge's note is hard to follow and that a clearer write-up should have come first. Alpöge says he intends to write the argument up properly, and expects shorter proofs to follow.


Outside mathematics, little changes right away. Scientific American notes that the proof[doesn't have any immediate real-world applications](https://www.scientificamerican.com/article/anthropic-mathematician-claims-to-prove-riemann-hypothesis-most-famous-problem-in-all-of-math/) and won't upend global banking.


## What does the Riemann proof mean for AI in 2027?


It shows AI doing original work at the top of a field, with an expert guiding it. Alpöge chose the approach, based on a simpler case he had worked through. Claude then handled areas of mathematics that Alpöge says he doesn't know well, and near the end it moved well ahead of him.


The pace has picked up too. The Navier-Stokes result and the Riemann proof landed in the same year, and the timeline in Alpöge's note runs from early October to November 16, about six weeks.


If AI can produce new knowledge in mathematics, fields that run on reasoning are likely to follow soon. Theoretical physics and computer science are limited mainly by how far people can think through a problem, much like math.


Fields tied to the physical world will move more slowly. A new drug or material still has to be made and tested, and those experiments take time however quickly the ideas arrive.


## What problems could AI solve next?


The likeliest candidates are other famous open problems, starting with the four Millennium Prize Problems that remain unsolved: P versus NP, the Hodge conjecture, the Yang-Mills problem and the Birch and Swinnerton-Dyer conjecture.


Problems close to the Riemann hypothesis are nearer still. Alpöge expects his method to reach the Extended Riemann Hypothesis, a further generalization of the problem, given more time.


Alpöge has also taken on problems outside number theory. Terence Tao[highlighted a proof](https://terrytao.wordpress.com/2026/11/20/unforced-euler-singularity-unforced-navier-stokes-singularity-and-the-generalized-riemann-hypothesis/) by Alpöge and two collaborators, written with heavy use of AI, showing that the equations describing how an ideal fluid moves, the same kind used to model air and water, can break down in a finite time. Like the Riemann proof, it is checked in Lean.


## What does the Riemann proof mean for ecommerce?


Mathematicians will take a long time to digest the proof, but one thing is already clear: AI has crossed from repeating knowledge to creating it. For ecommerce teams, that's a reason to revisit which work goes to AI and which stays with people.


The way the proof was made shows how that split can work. Alpöge knew the problem and chose the direction. Claude brought knowledge of areas he didn't know well, and took the work further than he could alone. In ecommerce, teams know their customers and their brand, and AI brings the knowledge and reach to act on that across the whole catalog.
